RagShortTexts: Rus law distinguishes debt service, rural people and household slaves rather than one status.
Debts, work, flight and masters’ duties require specific judgment and affect families.

Variants.Content:
Rus rural people occupy different positions in person and property; smerd, zakup and household slave are distinct legal terms. A debt servant’s borrowed money, goods or seed creates labour obligations whose amount and use matter. Working for another does not automatically place an entire family in hereditary ownership; disputes depend on status, events and applicable rules.

Debt links present food with future work, while a servant’s own fields and children also need care. Flight can have serious consequences, but a master’s abuse can also be disputed. Witnesses and a clear debt history shape the case. Poor harvests may force further borrowing, and help from neighbours can preserve a family’s sowing.
Creditors need clear debts and services rather than merged statuses. Taking all seed and working time can make repayment harder instead of increasing real returns.
Recruiters need to check existing duties rather than accept claims of freedom without inquiry. Clothing alone does not distinguish flight from lawful travel.
Seed loans save sowing but promised labour competes with home fields. Families need debt and work terms, while help from kin can prevent another loan.
